projects.title: SUBC Submarine Drivetrain
projects.cardSummary: Drivetrain design work focused on FEA-guided plate weight reduction and a machined frame backplate.
projects.summary: Contributed to SUBC's 2:1 contra-rotating drivetrain, with a focus on lighter gearbox plates and a frame backplate taken from CAD into the shop.
projects.goal: The drivetrain subteam designs and refines the pilot-to-propeller powertrain for SUBC's human-powered submarine. My focus was reducing plate mass while checking load paths and developing a frame backplate that could be drawn and machined.
projects.built: Developed spreadsheet-based gear-force and mounting-reaction load cases for SolidWorks static FEA, alongside AGMA gear calculations and DE-Goodman shaft fatigue analysis. Compared uncut, pocketed, and ribbed bottom-plate concepts; modeled the frame backplate in SolidWorks, prepared its dimensioned drawing, and worked on its machining.
projects.result: Compared a 2.35 lb uncut bottom-plate model with a 1.45 lb pocketed concept, a 38% modeled mass reduction, and also studied a 1.51 lb alternative. Produced the frame-backplate CAD model and machining drawing and brought the part into the mill while the team manufactured and assembled the drivetrain.
verifiedFacts: Designed a compact 2:1 straight-bevel gearbox for counter-rotating propellers.
Targeted 180 RPM through concentric, counter-rotating output shafts.
Used AGMA bevel-gear stress calculations and DE-Goodman shaft fatigue analysis.
Ran SolidWorks static FEA on the bevel gears and housing plates.

The small-bevel-pair spreadsheet uses the design report's nominal 110 W per propeller at 90 RPM and a 24:12 tooth pair, calculates 180 RPM output and 8.61/4.30 ft-lbf shaft torques, then resolves one gear-force case into 137.7 lbf tangential, 22.4 lbf radial, and 44.8 lbf axial components.

A separate bottom-plate spreadsheet starts with larger/smaller gear tangential inputs of 162.824/181.476 lbf; over a 5.75 in support span, it resolves the larger-gear input to 54.9 and 108.0 lbf reactions, then halves those values for two mounting holes at each location. The source workbooks do not document a direct handoff between their differing gear-force inputs.
Reduced modeled bottom-plate mass by 38%, from 2.35 lb to 1.45 lb.

Compared an uncut 2.35 lb bottom-plate model, a pocketed 1.45 lb concept, and a 1.51 lb alternative in SolidWorks stress studies; the images alone do not establish physical validation or a passing safety factor.
Modeled a frame backplate in SolidWorks, prepared a dimensioned drawing showing its recessed pocket, center bore, and four-hole pattern, and worked on machining the part.
Designed the housing around 6061-T6 plates and CNC manufacturing.
Manufactured and assembled the four-plate housing, 1144 carbon-steel bevel gears, concentric shafts, bearings, bushings, and retainers.
Used waterjet cutting and other shop machining processes while producing mechanical parts.
Spent 100+ hours modelling the gearbox and housing and completed 30+ structural and flow simulations.

projects.title: Star Solutions Engineering Internship
projects.cardSummary: Used SolidWorks and DFMA principles to take a chassis-mounted RF adapter through a 3D-printed fit check, three-sheet drawing, and finished metal part.
projects.summary: At Star Solutions, I designed one direct chassis-mounted NEX10-to-SMA adapter in SolidWorks to address an over-torque failure mode and eliminate an intermediate cable from the design. I checked a 3D-printed prototype, prepared a three-sheet manufacturing drawing, and received the metal part shown here. I also tested two four-way RF splitters at 4.01 GHz with a Keysight E5071C.
projects.goal: Apply design for manufacture and assembly (DFMA) to a direct panel-mounted RF connection: reduce intermediate hardware, account for chassis-wall thickness and inside-nut installation, and document a part a supplier could quote. Separately, verify two four-way splitters against RF datasheet limits at 4.01 GHz.
projects.built: Modeled the NEX10-to-SMA adapter in SolidWorks around panel thickness, nut access, thread engagement, and cable clearance. Produced a three-sheet manufacturing drawing and a 3D-printed fit check before receiving the finished metal part. Used a Keysight E5071C vector network analyzer to collect 24 insertion-loss, isolation, and VSWR measurements across two four-way splitters at 4.01 GHz, plus amplitude-unbalance values. Compared supplier quotations and mapped the COMPAC-N cable and block interfaces in Microsoft Visio.
projects.result: The finished metal adapter was manufactured and received; the photos document its progression from CAD and printed prototype to physical hardware, not production qualification. The splitter measurements averaged 2.0% deviation from datasheet typicals and passed applicable hard limits. Amplitude unbalance was 0.135 and 0.150 dB against a 0.6 dB maximum. Supplier prices of $18.71 per unit at MOQ 100 and $13.72 at MOQ 300, with four proposed samples and a 4–5-week lead time, were quoted terms rather than realized savings or purchases.
projects.disclosure: Completed as part of a Mechanical / Electrical Engineering internship. Earlier technical materials were reviewed and approved for public display by Star Solutions; the finished-part and chassis fit-check photos were supplied by Chiune.

projects.title: Sonous Systems — Echo
projects.subtitle: Acoustic Drone Detection
projects.cardSummary: Designing Echo acoustic sensing nodes and a mobile rover concept, from enclosure CAD and embedded audio to classification, bearing estimates, and operator views.
projects.summary: At Sonous Systems, I work on Echo: an acoustic drone-sensing platform spanning the sensing-node enclosure, embedded capture and detection software, bearing and multi-node concepts, and operator interfaces. The current Sonous site also introduces Mobile Echo, a rover concept that carries the node to a listening position.
projects.goal: Make an acoustic sensor that one person could place in a useful location, detect small drones by sound, report a bearing, and communicate uncertainty. The node must package microphones and electronics for deployment; the mobile concept must stop its own drive noise before listening.
projects.built: Designed the Echo node assembly in SolidWorks and worked through enclosure packaging, microphone placement, and internal component arrangement. On the software side, built a traceable audio dataset and leakage-aware evaluation pipeline, implemented six-channel prototype capture and raw-channel direction finding, and developed GPS/PPS-aware node messages, local-coordinate bearing fusion, and dashboard concepts. The new Sonous site presents a sealed four-microphone product direction and Mobile Echo rover imagery; that product description is distinct from the six-channel development prototype.
projects.result: An offline, license-safe YAMNet classification head reached 0.900 F1, 0.925 balanced accuracy, and 0.984 ROC-AUC across 90 out-of-fold recordings. The enclosure CAD and operator concepts show the intended system architecture. The Sonous site now presents fixed Echo and Mobile Echo concepts; quantitative field detection and localization performance are still unverified.
verifiedFacts: The source-traceable data pipeline covers 2,090 audio clips and 1,614 leakage groups.
A license-safe YAMNet classification head was evaluated with five-fold leakage-aware cross-validation.
Across 90 out-of-fold recordings, it reached 0.900 F1, 0.925 balanced accuracy, and 0.984 ROC-AUC.
A separate standardized benchmark covered 2,292 unique clips with no missing files.
The license-safe CC0 arm of that benchmark reached 0.9329 ROC-AUC and 0.2592 recall at a false-positive rate of at most 2%.
A research-only arm reached 0.9548 ROC-AUC and 0.6392 recall at a false-positive rate of at most 2%, but includes non-commercially licensed audio and must not be presented as a commercial model.
Initial PANNs/CNN14 baselines produced excessive false alarms and are not field-ready.
Six-channel audio capture, raw-channel direction finding, GPS/PPS-aware messages, robust local-ENU bearing fusion, and operator mapping are implemented in software.
The three-node fusion visual is a synthetic software demonstration, not a field result or measured localization-accuracy claim.
Sonous Systems is the startup name and Echo is the product name.
ECHO stands for Early Counter-drone Hearing Outpost.
The selected SolidWorks enclosure design is intended for each Echo sensing node; enclosure production remains in progress.
The dashboard concept includes a main operator view and small circular layouts intended for watches and other accessible devices; deployment remains planned.
The mobile physical node is practically finished and is entering field testing with encouraging early results.
Two stationary nodes are being built, and triangulation software is under development to complete the three-node prototype.
Quantitative field calibration and final field validation remain incomplete; no measured localization-accuracy claim has been established.
The current Sonous website describes Echo as a sealed four-microphone node that listens, classifies, and reports a bearing.
The current Sonous website introduces Mobile Echo as a rover carrying the same node; it halts before listening so its own drive noise does not mask incoming sound.
The supplied local as2-node-v9-assembly STEP file contains the Echo node enclosure assembly for an interactive CAD view.

projects.title: Radiator Conjugate Heat Transfer (CFD)
projects.cardSummary: A 903,945-element ANSYS Fluent study combining a quantitative convection baseline with explicit-air flow visualization.
projects.summary: Developed a simplified conjugate heat-transfer model of a serpentine radiator passage, preserved the working convection baseline, and added an external-air domain to visualize coolant-to-air heat transfer.
projects.goal: Build a defensible thermal-fluid workflow for studying how coolant flow and radiator-face air velocity affect heat removal, outlet temperature, and pressure drop.
projects.built: Created water and external-air fluid domains with aluminum shell conduction, a 1 mm tube wall, the energy equation, standard k-epsilon turbulence, coupled thermal boundaries, a 903,945-element tetrahedral mesh, report definitions, velocity vectors, and temperature contours.
projects.result: The simplified convection-boundary baseline converged from a 373 K coolant inlet to approximately 371.232 K at the outlet and estimated approximately 1.03 kW of heat removal at 0.13919 kg/s. The explicit-air case is retained as a qualitative visualization pending interface cleanup, fin/core representation, and formal validation.
verifiedFacts: Built a simplified ANSYS Fluent radiator model with a 903,945-element tetrahedral mesh.
Modelled water and external-air fluid domains with aluminum shell conduction and a 1 mm tube wall.
Enabled the energy equation and standard k-epsilon turbulence model.
The convection-boundary baseline used a 373 K coolant inlet at 0.5 m/s and converged to approximately 371.232 K at the outlet.
The reported coolant mass flow was approximately 0.13919 kg/s and the simplified baseline estimated approximately 1.03 kW of heat removal.
Preserved the working convection-boundary case before developing the explicit-air visualization model.
The modelling workflow began from imported shell geometry for the serpentine tube and radiator fins.
Created velocity-vector and temperature-contour visualizations for the external-air case.
The explicit-air model is qualitative until interface warnings are resolved, the fin/core effect is represented, and mass/energy balance plus mesh-independence checks are completed.
The planned air-speed and coolant-flow sensitivity runs have not yet been completed.
